author: Biswajit Panda
headline: Data Engineering & Analytics | Kafka · Airflow · PostgreSQL · Power BI | Building Real-Time Pipelines
text:
🚨 Most people FAIL this SQL interview question — not because it’s hard… but because they think about it the wrong way.
👉 Problem:
Find employees who earn MORE than their department’s average salary.
❌ Where people go wrong:
• Mixing row-level data with aggregated data
• Adding emp_id inside a grouped CTE (🚫 logic break)
• Confusing table aliases (c.salary vs e.salary)
• Trying to solve everything in one messy query
• Not separating the problem into clear steps
✅ The correct thinking (this is what interviewers look for):
1️⃣ First → Calculate average salary per department
2️⃣ Then → Join it back to employees
3️⃣ Next → Compare each employee’s salary
4️⃣ Finally → Filter those earning above average
💡 This is why CTEs are powerful:
They turn complex logic into clean, readable steps.
🧠 Clean Solution:
WITH cte AS (
 SELECT department, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary
 FROM employees
 GROUP BY department
)
SELECT e.emp_id, e.department, e.salary
FROM cte c
JOIN employees e
 ON c.department = e.department
WHERE e.salary > c.avg_salary;
✨ Simple query.
💥 Powerful interview pattern.
📌 Easy to mess up if your fundamentals aren’t clear.
💬 How would YOU explain this to a beginner?
Or… can you solve it without using a CTE?

author: Ekta Patel
headline: Entry-Level Data Analyst | SQL | Advanced Excel | Customer Data Analysis | Reporting & Dashboards | Immediate Joiner
text:
🚀 SQL Practice | Real Interview Scenario

Today I worked on an interesting SQL problem:

👉 Find customers who purchased both “Laptop” and “Mobile”

At first glance, it looks simple using IN ('Laptop','Mobile'), but that only filters rows — it doesn’t guarantee that a customer bought both products.

💡 The real challenge:
We need to identify customers who have purchased both categories, not just either one.

🧠 My Approach:
I used:
GROUP BY → to group data at customer level
HAVING → to filter aggregated results
COUNT(DISTINCT product) → to ensure both products exist

✅ Solution:
SELECT customer_id, customer_name 
FROM sales_orders
WHERE product IN ('Laptop','Mobile')
GROUP BY customer_id, customer_name
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT product) > 1;

🔍 Key Insight:
👉 COUNT(DISTINCT product) > 1 ensures the customer purchased both Laptop AND Mobile

📈 What I learned:
Difference between row-level filtering vs group-level filtering
Importance of HAVING in solving real business problems
How small logic changes can completely change the result

If you have solved this differently, would love to see your approach 👇

Design Challenge:

→ Batch vs. real-time processing — when to use what and why
